extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and public administration; policymakers interested in party organization and administrative reform
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical criteria for evaluating how party organization, administrative structure, and forms of government (cabinet vs. presidential) affect administrative efficiency, popular responsiveness, and democratic practice. The page outlines causes, consequences, and reforms related to party dominance, centralization, and boss rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: National_vs_personal_representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which an elected representative acts as the personal rather than the political representative of constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by anecdotes (French deputies receiving personal requests); where national party influence is weak and local parties dominate, representatives tend to serve local/personal interests. Contrast: in systems with strong national parties, candidates owe allegiance primarily to the party and its platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local_party_dominance_and_patron-client_relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When local parties predominate, politics tends toward patronage: politicians acting as 'fairy godfathers' who provide personal favors to constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bailing people out of police courts, obtaining jobs, distributing coal; such patron-client relations are based on self-interest and tend to misuse governmental power for class or personal advantage (described as medieval/feudal lord-vassal relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: National_parties_as_means_to_realize_principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong national parties can realize political principles held by a large portion of the population, despite sometimes becoming self-perpetuating machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges abuses (machines, self-advancement) but argues national parties still give allegiance to party principles and can press executives for party ends; candidates primarily further party platform rather than only local interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative_function_separated_from_political_influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative efficiency can be obtained only by recognizing an administrative function that should be discharged free from political influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues for an administrative function insulated from politics to improve efficiency; anti-pattern: mixing political influence into administrative tasks reduces efficiency and responsiveness to the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization_and_permanence_for_administrative_efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable centralization of the administrative system and greater permanence in tenure of administrative officers facilitate recognition and discharge of an independent administrative function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: centralization and stable tenure help administrative officers perform functions free from political fluctuations; presented as remedies to administrative inefficiency caused by party influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party_responsiveness_to_public_will
rubrics_metrics.description: For government to be popular, parties that lack popular confidence must be able to retire from power and party leaders who have forfeited confidence must be removable from control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: existence of mechanisms allowing a party or its leaders to be replaced when they lose public confidence. Without these, government cannot be truly popular. Examples: English practice where ministers resign when they lose parliamentary approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits_of_popular_conscious_deliberation_in_complex_societies
rubrics_metrics.description: In populous, heterogeneous, extended polities, the formal institutions do not generally provide for conscious deliberation by the people; extra-governmental organizations (parties) exercise controlling influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: democratic ideals of conscious public deliberation are often unrealizable in complex modern states; evaluation should consider the role of parties and extra-constitutional devices in shaping policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties_may_become_ends_in_themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties often shift from instruments for certain ends to ends in themselves, with party allegiance replacing adherence to political principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: perpetuation of party becomes primary motive; members' role reduces to amending or negating leaders' propositions rather than initiating policy. Anti-pattern: party cohesion for its own sake undermines principled politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity_of_leaders_who_originated_policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because parties are formed for action rather than debate, they require leaders capable of originating policies acceptable to the membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: parties tend to follow leaders rather than lead; this dynamic explains reduced opportunity for broad internal debate and can concentrate power in leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet_government_promotes_coordination_and_responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet (parliamentary) government unites legislative and administrative functions in ministers who both formulate and execute policy and are responsible to Parliament and thus to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: simplicity, flexibility, easier ascertainment of public opinion through Parliament, and clearer responsibility because officials in law are those exercising political power. Example: English system where ministers guide legislation and administration and resign when losing parliamentary approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility_of_unwritten_constitutions_and_precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems like England's, with flexible forms fixed largely by statute and precedent rather than entrenched written law, permit gradual institutional adaptations (e.g., development of the Cabinet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: such flexibility allows governmental organs to take on new functions by precedent; courts do not rigidly protect form, facilitating political development along 'lines of least resistance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential_systems_impede_immediate_responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A presidential (separated) system is less able than cabinet government to respond immediately to shifts in public opinion because the executive is independently elected and constitutional arrangements fix terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: differences between legislative and executive branches can't be settled until elections; constitutional rigidity makes adaptation slow; parties must become stronger and more permanent to coordinate government, risking deadlock and reduced responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength_and_permanence_of_parties_reduce_internal_responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Although parties must be strong and often permanent to coordinate across separated institutions, this very strength and permanence make party organizations less responsive to the party membership's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members often tolerate arbitrary leader action to preserve party success; fear of weakening the party leads to acceptance of reduced leader accountability; this is a tradeoff between effectiveness in government and internal democratic responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary_and_caucus_structure_affects_democratic_nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of primaries and caucuses determines whether party nominations are democratic or controlled by parlor caucuses/committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rural New England primaries retain town-meeting character with discussion and chance to break slates; elsewhere primaries become mere polling-places selecting delegates, enabling secret parlor caucuses or political clubs to make real nominations. Reform of primary methods is presented as the key point of attack to improve party responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration_of_party_control_in_a_single_boss
rubrics_metrics.description: The control of party organizations by a single person (the 'boss') undermines popular government and political responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: bosses exert extensive, often hidden power (e.g., 'Do this, and he doeth it'), may avoid holding public office, and can steer nominations and appointments. This concentration is judged dangerous to the ideals of popular government.
